title: Why Trade-offs Hide in Natural Data

scenes.tts: Strap a harness onto a breeding skylark. It adds three to four grams, about a tenth of the bird's body mass. Its nest tends to produce fewer fledglings. Yet nobody took any food away. So where did the chicks go?

scenes.tts: Every organism works from a limited budget. Energy and nutrients are split among growth, maintenance and repair, storage, and reproduction. Like a monthly paycheck, more for one means less for another. That negative link is a trade-off. So a cost paid out of a fixed budget may leave less for young, for upkeep, or for both.
scenes.visual: A budget bar split four ways; reproduction grows as maintenance shrinks; a dashed, hedged cost block squeezes the rest.

scenes.tts: Now the puzzle. In many bird populations, birds with big clutches survive better. That does not refute a trade-off. Some individuals acquire more than others. A bird that gathers more can afford more eggs and a longer life. So across birds, the link is positive. For any one bird, though, more spent on eggs still leaves less for itself.
scenes.visual: Two budget bars, big and small; across them eggs and survival rise together; inside the big bar the divider moves.

scenes.tts: To see the trade-off, change one thing on purpose. Enlarge a brood. Add a handicap. Add back one nutrient. Now take a meta-analysis of thirty bird species. Naturally larger clutches went with better parental survival. Enlarged broods lowered survival on average, with a small effect. But the interval for each added chick includes zero. So a fixed cost per extra egg is not supported.

scenes.tts: Now the skylark numbers, from first broods. Nineteen of twenty five control nests succeeded. Eight of seventeen handicapped nests did. That is seventy six percent against forty seven point one percent. The gap is twenty eight point nine percentage points. Measured against the control rate, it is a thirty eight point one percent reduction. Those are two different numbers. Percentage points compare two rates directly. Percent compares one rate to the other. Mean fledglings per nest fell from two point zero to one point two.
scenes.caption: Now the skylark numbers, from first broods. 19 of 25 control nests succeeded. 8 of 17 handicapped nests did. That is 76.0% against 47.1%. The gap is 28.9 percentage points. Measured against the control rate, it is a 38.1% reduction. Those are two different numbers. Percentage points compare two rates directly. Percent compares one rate to the other. Mean fledglings per nest fell from 2.0 to 1.2.

scenes.tts: So the harness and load together reduced reproductive output in this population. The nest success gap was borderline. The study did not establish a survival cost to the adults. And no group wore a harness alone, so harness and load cannot be separated. Keep this rule. A natural correlation can hide a trade-off, so change one thing on purpose and compare with controls.
